I am no expert on this, but it is based on opponency in color perception as far as I know. Basically the way the receptors for the colors red, blue, and green integrate has to do with overall luminance, red-green relationships, and blue-yellow relationships.

There are three types of neuronal fibers. One set responds to red-green color differences. A (+)Red(-)Green neuron would increase it's neuronal output in the presence of red light, and decrease output in the presence of green light. A (-)Red(+)Green does the exact opposite. The second set has the same relationships, just involving Blue-Yellow. The third set for luminance perception is black-white difference.

When a set of neurons fatigues from too much output, it's output will decrease. If it's a (+)Red(-)Green neuron, the decrease in activity will be interpreted by the brain as an increase in green light, and so the "after effect" once you look away is to see the original neuronal output in the negative color: green, when you shut your eyes briefly.

Taken cumulatively on a color inverted image like the one in the OP, your neurons will tire after about 30 seconds of looking and when you look away, the after effect is to see the color negative.

This - but file as 3 entities.

Start an llc. That is your wood working business.

Start another llc that buys and owns ALL the equipment and tools. This company leases the equipment to your woodworking company.

If woodworking company or non-profit ever gets sued, they have ZERO assets.

The llc that owns all the tools can't be touched. You would never lose equipment over lawsuit and could always open a new llc for woodworking and bankrupt the other one.

Start a non-profit. This is your classes open to the public for free (once a month). This also gets people in the door to buy products and see what you've built.

The non-profit will allow you to accept used equipment and donations of tools and supplies (those who donate can write it off).

So your llc donates time, space, tools, etc to your non-profit. And you can write that off for your business.
